lesson.title: One Expression, Many Faces: Simplifying to Its Simplest Form
lesson.summary: Simplifying an expression means using the order of operations and combining like terms to rewrite it in an equivalent form with as few terms and operations as possible.
lesson.body:
Two expressions can look completely different on paper and still be exactly the same for every value you plug in. That is the whole point of simplifying: taking an expression and rewriting it as an equivalent one that is shorter and easier to work with, without changing what it actually equals. You already know how to evaluate an expression by substituting a number for each variable and computing the result. Simplifying uses that same idea in reverse, as a way to check your work: if you simplify correctly, the original expression and the simplified one must evaluate to the same number for any input you choose.

The process itself leans heavily on combining like terms. First, use the order of operations to make sure any grouped or nested arithmetic is handled correctly. Then scan the expression for terms with matching variable parts and combine their coefficients, exactly as you practiced when combining like terms on its own. What is left after every possible combination has been made is the simplified form. There is no single fixed number of terms an expression must reach; it is simplified once no two remaining terms can be combined any further.

Let's simplify 5x - 3 + 2x - x + 8 - 4x. Group the x terms first: 5x, 2x, -x, and -4x. Adding their coefficients gives 5 + 2 - 1 - 4 = 2, so the combined x term is 2x. Now group the constants: -3 and 8, which add to 5. Putting the pieces together, the simplified expression is 2x + 5. To check this, substitute x = 1 into both versions. The original gives 5(1) - 3 + 2(1) - 1 + 8 - 4(1) = 5 - 3 + 2 - 1 + 8 - 4 = 7, and the simplified version gives 2(1) + 5 = 7. Since both equal 7, the simplification is correct. Trying a second value, x = 3, gives 15 - 3 + 6 - 3 + 8 - 12 = 11 for the original and 2(3) + 5 = 11 for the simplified form, which matches again.

Simplifying also applies when exponents are involved, as long as the exponents on matching variable parts are identical. Consider 4x^2 - 3x^2 + 5x - 2 + x. The two x^2 terms combine first: 4x^2 - 3x^2 = (4 - 3)x^2 = x^2. The two x terms combine next: 5x + x = 5x + 1x = 6x. Only the constant -2 has nothing to combine with, so it stays as is. The simplified expression is x^2 + 6x - 2. Checking at x = 2, the original gives 4(2)^2 - 3(2)^2 + 5(2) - 2 + 2 = 16 - 12 + 10 - 2 + 2 = 14, and the simplified form gives (2)^2 + 6(2) - 2 = 4 + 12 - 2 = 14. Both equal 14, so the simplification checks out.

It helps to double check with more than one value of x, because a single matching value could occur by coincidence even if a mistake was made elsewhere in the expression. Two matching checks at different values make an error far less likely to slip through unnoticed.

A frequent mistake is combining terms whose variable parts are not actually identical, such as merging a plain x term with an x^2 term, or losing track of a negative sign that belongs to the term right after it. Simplifying carefully, one term at a time, avoids both problems. Once an expression is fully simplified, it becomes much easier to evaluate for different inputs, compare to other expressions, and eventually use inside an equation, which is exactly why this skill sits at the center of so much algebra work.
